23-year-old Azerbaijani artist dies after stabbing attack, stepbrother detained
articles.summary: A 23-year-old Azerbaijani artist, Gulara Mehdiyeva, has died in hospital after being stabbed at her home in Baku
articles.body: A 23-year-old Azerbaijani artist, Gulara Mehdiyeva, has died in hospital after being stabbed at her home in Baku. Her 18-year-old stepbrother has reportedly been detained in connection with the attack, with neighbours suggesting he had demanded she remove photos from her social media, which men were commenting on, prior to the assault. Police received a report that a 23-year-old woman had been injured with a sharp object on Monday in Baku’s Binagadi district. According to a report by Real TV , Mehdiyeva’s neighbours said she was seriously injured and alone for around two hours after the attack. Her father reportedly found her lying on the floor covered in blood after returning home. He took her to the hospital, but Mehidyeva later succumbed to her injuries. The neighbours also claimed to a local outlet that her stepbrother, Aykhan Mehdiyev, had planned the attack several days beforehand, claiming that the siblings had previously had disagreements — including that he had demanded that Gulara delete photos from her social media, which men were commenting on. The suspect was detained by police and handed over to investigators, according to Azerbaijani media reports. The Binagadi District Prosecutor’s Office has launched a criminal investigation into the incident, which is ongoing. Gulara Mehdiyeva was a young amateur artist who shared her artwork on social media, particularly Instagram, where she had around 3,000 followers. Her work included decorative 3D mandala art, using dot-painting techniques, as well as oil paintings on canvas, with a focus on femininity. Rafiq Shahbazov is a journalist based in Tbilisi, covering political and social developments in Azerbaijan, as well as issues affecting ethnic Azerbaijanis in the region. He has worked with independent media outlets. His work focuses on human rights, environmental issues, and pressure on journalists and civil society.

articles.title: US Envoys See Ukraine Peace Progress As NATO Debate Resurfaces
articles.summary: But Russia cast doubt on that assertion and talks involving Ukrainian and Western officials in Berlin left major questions unresolved
articles.body: WASHINGTON -- US and European officials have edged closer to unity on a Ukraine peace framework, with Washington open to NATO-style security guarantees and US envoy Jared Kushner saying Moscow may be receptive to the idea. But Russia cast doubt on that assertion and talks involving Ukrainian and Western officials in Berlin left major questions unresolved, including how Ukraine would be protected against another Russian attack, whether its territorial integrity would be preserved, and what concessions might be required for a settlement. As European leaders push for a role in peace negotiations alongside the US, Ukraine, and Russia, US envoy Steve Witkoff said “important work remains.” Witkoff, who attended the Berlin meeting on November 19 along with Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, described the discussions as “frank and productive.” He said Trump was determined to end the war in a way that preserves Ukraine's security and sovereignty and prevents a recurrence of conflict. The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries coordinating military and other support for Ukraine, was hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and other leaders. It sought to strengthen Western support for Kyiv and secure a European role in US-led peace efforts. Kushner offered an indication of the US administration's thinking on Ukraine's postwar security, saying Washington had made progress in securing Russian acceptance of the idea of an Article 5-style guarantee -- a commitment modeled on NATO's collective-defense clause, under which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. “From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal,” he said, adding that Trump was open to the idea, provided it served US interests and formed part of a broader security package. Kushner said Washington had made Moscow “comfortable” with the concept, arguing that Russia also wanted to avoid another war after the current conflict. He acknowledged, however, that skepticism remained about Moscow's intentions. Russia, which wants any peace deal to include a bar on Ukraine ever joining NATO, threw cold water on the idea that Moscow might accept an arrangement that included Article 5-like guarantees for Ukraine. "I want to say that even finding a formula for 'quasi-membership' in NATO for Kyiv -- or seeking some sort of, in quotation marks, 'creative solution' in this area -- is an unacceptable option for us," Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on November 20. Kyiv and the West "should acknowledge the nonnegotiable nature of our demand that [Ukraine] must not join NATO," the Russian news agency Interfax quoted Ryabkov as saying. "Once that happens, I believe the question of security guarantees could, in one way or another, be discussed." Pentagon Official Says Ukraine War Likely To Last Through Winter, Despite Mediation Efforts An Article 5-like guarantee could replicate elements of NATO's collective-defense commitment without making Ukraine a member of the alliance. Its credibility would depend on the legal obligations, military arrangements, and the willingness of participating countries to respond to another Russian attack. Zelenskyy said Ukraine would like more clarity on what such a guarantee would involve. "I'm not sure that we have a common [understanding] of Article 5," he said, adding that for him, it means "that there some forces of partners on your land" and suggesting that in his view, US and European forces should be based in Ukraine. Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron urged Ukraine's allies to reconsider NATO membership rather than rely exclusively on alternative security arrangements. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO,” Macron said. Macron also called for urgent deliveries of air-defense systems and interceptors to protect Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure from Russian missile and drone attacks. A joint statement following the Berlin meeting by the leaders of Germany, France, Britain, and Ukraine reaffirmed that Kyiv must receive robust, legally binding security guarantees once a cease-fire takes effect. The proposed framework could include sustained military, financial and technical assistance, participation in a US-led cease-fire monitoring mechanism and a European-led multinational force supported by Washington. Wider Europe Briefing: Europe's Fruitless Search For A Ukraine Peace Envoy; EU Safeguards For Montenegro The force could provide reassurance measures on land, at sea and in the air while helping consolidate Ukraine's armed forces. The leaders also envisaged a legally binding commitment, subject to national procedures, to take measures to restore peace and security if Russia attacks again. Moscow vocally opposes Western troop deployments in Ukraine as part of security guarantees, a position President Vladimir Putin repeated this week. The joint statement stressed that Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity and right to choose its security arrangements must be respected. It also rejected changing international borders by force. The coalition pledged continued military and financial support for Kyiv and increased economic pressure on Moscow, including measures targeting Russian energy revenues, cryptocurrency transactions, illicit financial flows, and its military-industrial complex. The European leaders also called for an energy cease-fire during the winter and an arrangement to protect food exports through the Black Sea, as Russian attacks threaten Ukraine's power supplies and the war continues to disrupt maritime trade. Putin Has Shown No Willingness To End Ukraine War, Says Mike Pompeo Merz said further peace negotiations were expected soon, with Europe participating alongside the US, Russia, and Ukraine. He suggested the United Arab Emirates as a possible neutral venue. Kushner said Trump wanted an agreement developed with European and Ukrainian participation, not imposed unilaterally by Washington. “President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” he said. The diplomatic efforts are unfolding amid growing criticism in Washington of Trump's recent engagement with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Trump met Putin and Xi at an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, which produced no breakthrough on ending Russia's war in Ukraine. A joint US-Chinese-Russian statement made no mention of the war. The senior Democrat in the US Senate, Chuck Schumer, dismissed the trilateral meeting as a diplomatic embarrassment, arguing that Trump had secured no meaningful commitments on Ukraine or international security. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Senate Democrat on foreign policy, said defeating Putin in Ukraine remained essential to US national security. Trump, Xi, And Putin Make History, But No Breakthroughs: 4 Takeaways From The Trilateral Summit Representative Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee in the House of Representatives, said the summit had not advanced nuclear nonproliferation, ended Russia's war, or addressed Chinese human rights abuses. Republican Senator Thom Tillis also questioned the intentions of Moscow and Beijing, while Representative Don Bacon criticized Trump's approach, saying Republicans had traditionally stood up to Russia and China. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine introduced a resolution seeking answers from the administration about purchases of Russian fuel, sanctions relief, and delays in delivering air-defense munitions to Ukraine. He argued that buying Russian fuel risked providing Moscow with revenue to finance its war.

articles.title: Boy, 7, pulled alive from rubble hours after Russian strike on Ukraine, rescuers say
articles.summary: Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said
articles.body: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes hit Kyiv A seven-year-old boy has been rescued from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in the Kyiv region, after 14 hours. Overnight Russian strikes on the village killed 11 people, Ukrainian officials have said. The attack occurred in the early hours of Sunday. A 79-year-old woman was also rescued alive from the collapsed building, Kyiv's regional head Tymur Tkachenko said. A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 wounded in a separate strike on Vyshneve, also in the Kyiv region, that hit a grocery store on Sunday. Ukrainian authorities said the boy in Dymer is in stable condition and was taken to hospital, and have thanked everyone involved in saving his life. Zelensky and Ukraine's national police also confirmed the rescue of the boy. In a telegram post, Tkachenko said the 79-year-old woman rescued from the rubble was receiving treatment in hospital. Earlier he said six people were injured in the attack, while others were still missing. The attack on the residential building occurred in the early hours of the morning while people were asleep Zelensky said more than 130 people are involved in emergency operations at the scene, and that they will continue until they have "complete information about every single person". Sending his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed, he said the strike struck the residential building, "practically blowing a section of it to smithereens". Zelensky added that "rescue efforts are complicated by constant new air raid alerts and renewed threats". The strike hit the building at 05:00 local time, when families were still asleep, Ukraine's minister of internal affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi said. More than 70 strikes have been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, Vyhivskyi added. Emergency workers continue to search for those missing after Russian drone and missile attacks in Dymer. In his video address posted online, Zelensky also said three people were killed and 13 injured in a strike on an "ordinary grocery store" in Vyshneve. Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on social media that three children were among the injured. Italy: Workers and students stage nationwide strike over living costs
articles.summary: Protester Giorgia Giordani faulted the government’s handling of surging energy bills and everyday household expenses
articles.body: From the shadow of Rome’s Colosseum to major squares in Milan , Turin , Naples and Palermo , tens of thousands of workers and students took to the streets across more than 100 Italian cities as a 24-hour general strike disrupted schools, hospitals and public transport. Called by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL , alongside grassroots unions such as Cobas , the mobilisation coincided with an international student protest day in over 45 cities and a wider European day of action over living costs, military spending and the climate crisis. Carrying banners declaring "Education builds, war destroys" and "Funds for schools, not for war" through Rome’s historic centre, demonstrators demanded higher wages, stronger social protections and public investment instead of defence outlays. Protester Giorgia Giordani faulted the government’s handling of surging energy bills and everyday household expenses, while a student outside La Sapienza University said crowds wanted answers, and that some were demanding the government’s resignation, echoing CGIL Secretary-General Maurizio Landini’s call for sweeping reform of Italy’s social and economic model.

articles.title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
articles.summary: Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said
articles.body: An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said. The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government. Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured people from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said. The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation". "Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X. , external Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port. US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible. The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement. Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added. GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders. Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media. GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets". Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments. Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow. Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI). "Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians." If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast. As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui. But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army. Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians." EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
articles.summary: European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit
articles.body: European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit. This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU. During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era. He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction." Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances." He went further and said " Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people. Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime." She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers." Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries. She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much." Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it." In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election. "Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels. The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements. No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students "There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said. Von der Leyen ‌said ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,." On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules. They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes. According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation. Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues. The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit . Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit. Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

articles.title: Constitutional Court of BiH: Republika Srpska Can’t Ban the Insignia of the Army of RBiH
articles.summary: The challenged provision of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Official Gazette of Republika Srpska Nos
articles.body: At the session, the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina ruled that the provision of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, which criminalizes the display and glorification of the symbols, the flag and the insignia of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is unconstitutional! Among other things, the Court confirmed that its insignia belong to the military heritage of the Armed Forces of BiH and that their use is grounded in valid state regulations. “In this case, the Constitutional Court decided on the requests of eleven members of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Denis Bećirović, at the time of submitting a request, Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Denis Zvizdić, at the time of submitting a request, the First Deputy Chair of the House of Representatives of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for a review of the constitutionality of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska. The challenged provision of Article 359b of the Criminal Code of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Official Gazette of Republika Srpska Nos. 64/17, 104/18 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 15/21, 89/21, http://www.ohr.int – High Representative Decision No. 12/23, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ No. 73/23, ‘Official Gazette of BiH’ No. 9/24 – Constitutional Court of BiH Decision, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ Nos. 105/24 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 19/25, 31/25, ‘Official Gazette of BiH’ No. 36/25 – Constitutional Court of BiH Decision, ‘Official Gazette of Republika Srpska’ Nos. 85/25 – Constitutional Court of RS Decision, 92/25 – Law on the Cessation of Validity of Laws, 25/26, and 78/26) criminalized the public display, showing, production, reproduction, or in any way putting into circulation of flags, symbols, insignia, greetings, or slogans that promote or glorify the Army of RBiH. The Constitutional Court concluded that the provision of Article 359 b of the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska is not in line with Articles I(2) and III(3)(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In its reasoning for the decision, the Constitutional Court, among other things, emphasized that the challenged provision is not aligned with the laws regarding the use of official symbols and insignia of the Army of RBiH. The regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina regarding the appearance and the use of symbols and insignia of the Army of RBiH continue to apply on the territory of BiH based on the constitutional principle of continuity approved by Article I(1) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in conjunction with Article 2 of Annex II to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The National Assembly has no jurisdiction to decide on the cessation of validity of legal acts of the institutions of RBiH, whose continuity is constitutionally recognized. The challenged provision is therefore not aligned with Article III (3)(b) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in light of the continuity of legal provisions, as it disrupts the normative hierarchy which the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina unequivocally established in Article III (3) (b) through the harmonization of legal regulations within the legal systems according to their hierarchy, in which state laws must be aligned with the decisions of the institutions of BiH. In addition to this, pursuant to the decisions of the institutions of BiH, the Army of RBiH is part of the Armed Forces of BiH with its military heritage and identity, along with recognizable insignia, the display of which constitutes a duty for the respective infantry regiments. Therefore, the challenged provision is not aligned with Article I(2) of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina because it violates the decisions of the institutions of BiH requiring members of the regiment to wear their regimental insignia.”

articles.body: Five members of the National Liberation Army (ELN) rebel group have been killed in a bombing operation in southwestern Colombia, APA reports, citing Xinhua. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella confirmed on Sunday that the operation took place in the municipality of Dagua, in the department of Valle del Cauca. "In this operation, five members of the criminal structure commanded by alias 'Bertha' were killed, a leader for whom a reward of up to 787 million pesos (about 225,000 U.S. dollars) is offered," the president said. He added that a large quantity of ammunition and weapons had also been seized. According to De la Espriella, the ELN structure is responsible for 68 targeted killings, 72 cases of recruitment of minors, 55 extortions, 18 forced displacements and 10 attacks in southwestern Colombia. "My order is clear: maintain the offensive, regain territorial control and eliminate the narco-terrorist structures that threaten our farmers, merchants and transporters," he warned. The Colombian president also condemned a recent explosive attack in the department of Cesar, which killed one soldier and injured 12 others. Since taking office on August 7, De la Espriella has ordered seven bombing raids against various armed criminal and rebel groups in Catatumbo and other regions, including Guaviare and Choco. The operations have targeted the two main dissident factions of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the National Liberation Army and the Clan del Golfo criminal organization.

articles.title: No one in Chisinau listens to people who call for gas talks with Russia — former MP
articles.summary: Commenting on a public opinion poll held in October-November
articles.body: MOSCOW, November 23. /TASS/. The Moldovan government will not heed the people, the majority of whom supports talks with Russia on natural gas supplies, because they are following clear instructions of the European Union, Marina Tauber, executive committee secretary of Moldova’s Victory opposition bloc and former member of the republic’s parliament, told TASS. Commenting on a public opinion poll held in October-November, which showed that 69% of the people support the negotiations, she said: "They [the Moldovan authorities] haven’t heeded anything up until now, and they won’t heed anything now. They have clear instructions on this matter from the European Union. It’s very simple: if they wanted to heed it, they would have done so long ago. Initially, both the opposition and the business community, and all sectors, expressed [the view] that the first thing that needed to be done was to talk with [Russian President] Vladimir Vladimirovich [Putin] about gas supplies. And this was said at all levels. They won’t do it because the Europeans won’t allow them to. Gazprom stopped gas supplies to Moldova at the beginning of 2025 after a ban on its transit through Ukrainian territory and Chisinau’s refusal to resolve the issue of a $709 million debt for previously consumed fuel. In this situation the Moldovan State District Power Plant in Transnistria, which runs on Russian gas and supplied up to 70% of Moldova’s electricity needs, serves only consumers on the left bank of the Dniester River. In September, the Moldovan parliament introduced the state of emergency in the energy and hydrology sectors, while the government urged the people to save gas and electricity.

articles.title: Previously rejected Uzbek family ends 2-year church sanctuary after new asylum bid
articles.summary: According to the organization, church asylum coordinator Herman Stomphorst said Asylum Seekers (COA) is arranging accommodation for them
articles.body: The Uzbek Babayants family will leave the Open Hof church in Kampen within a few days, where they have received church sanctuary for the past two years. According to the organization, church asylum coordinator Herman Stomphorst said Asylum Seekers (COA) is arranging accommodation for them. “Until then, they may stay here in the church,” Stomphorst said shortly before the continuous church service ended on Saturday afternoon. The family of four children has lived in the Netherlands since 2014. Because they have now submitted a new residence application, the family may legally remain in the Netherlands for the duration of the procedure. The family itself chose to leave the church, supported by a ruling from the Council of State. In July, the Council of State ruled that three asylum-seeker families with children who have lived in the Netherlands for years and built lives here may stay. The highest administrative court determined that the minister must give greater weight to the interests of the children. For Stomphorst, Saturday is a tense day. “I worry that the procedure will take a very long time,” he said. “But I am reassured because the Council of State has been very clear.” At the same time, he is prepared for the possibility that things may not turn out well. “We are not naive. There is certainly a chance that the Immigration and Naturalisation Service (IND) will reject the application again. The Babayants family only submitted a new application this week, according to the family’s lawyer, Inge Zuidhoek, because it had to be properly prepared. Additional information was included about the family and their roots in the Netherlands. Zuidhoek hopes this new information will lead to a fresh assessment by the IND. “If it had no chance of success, I would not have submitted a new application,” she said.

articles.body: The Supreme Court / Yonhap A representative of judges nationwide has strongly criticized the ruling Democratic Party of Korea's push to impeach the Supreme Court chief justice, calling on his fellow judges to stand up against any attempt to undermine judicial independence. Kang Dong-won, a senior judge at the Seoul Family Court who also chairs the National Conference of Judge Representatives, issued the rebuke in a message posted on the court's internal network, CourtNet, on Sunday, accusing the DPK of "going beyond the bounds." The DPK announced its decision to seek the impeachment of Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae after the top court on Thursday partially overturned an appellate ruling that sentenced former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo to 15 years in prison for playing a key role in former President Yoon Suk Yeol's failed martial law bid. The ruling party has since dropped Thursday's ruling from its list of impeachment grounds, instead citing the top court's alleged compliance with Yoon's martial law declaration, its decision to send President Lee Jae Myung's election law case back to the appeals court and other allegations. "The extent to which certain political circles have recently encroached on judicial independence is alarming. I find myself wondering how much longer we are expected to put up with this," Kang said in the post titled "Regret over infringements on judicial independence." "We do not necessarily agree with everything the chief justice has done during his tenure. However, seeking his impeachment over a particular ruling goes beyond the bounds. If judges were impeached every time a ruling displeased someone, judicial independence would collapse." Kang warned that judges could begin taking political reactions into account when issuing rulings if such a precedent were set. Seeking to impeach the chief justice over a Supreme Court ruling amounts to an attempt to impeach the top court itself and exert undue pressure on the entire judiciary, he said, urging judges to actively stand up against attempts to infringe upon the independence of the judiciary. "If they ultimately vote for impeachment, shouldn't we also take 'action'?" he said, adding, "There are various ways we could respond. I believe we should not simply stand by in silence." The National Conference of Judge Representatives has decided to bring forward its regular meeting from Dec. 7 to next Monday.

articles.summary: Yonhap Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seocho District, Seoul, Friday
articles.body: Rep. Yang Bu-nam, center, who leads the ruling Democratic Party of Korea’s task force on impeaching Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae, speaks at a press briefing in the party leader’s office at the National Assembly, Sunday. Yonhap Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae arrives for work at the Supreme Court in Seocho District, Seoul, Friday. Yonhap The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) laid out its grounds Sunday for impeaching Supreme Court Chief Justice Cho Hee-dae and said it would seek a National Assembly vote by the end of December, drawing criticism that the move could undermine judicial independence. At its first public briefing at the Assembly, the party’s impeachment task force pointed to the Supreme Court’s handling of President Lee Jae Myung’s election law case and Cho’s refusal to recommend a new candidate for a vacant Supreme Court seat. “We will do our utmost to finalize the impeachment motion as quickly as possible and bring it to a vote in the National Assembly before the end of December,” said Rep. Yang Bu-nam, who leads the task force. He did not give a date for filing the motion. Other grounds previously raised by the party include the court’s response to the Dec. 3, 2024, martial law declaration, allegations over court operating expenses and cash payments, and Cho’s refusal to testify before the Assembly. The DPK made pursuing Cho’s impeachment its official position Friday, a day after the Supreme Court sent former Prime Minister Han Duck-soo’s insurrection case back to the Seoul High Court. The court found insufficient evidence that Han intended to subvert the constitutional order when he urged then-President Yoon Suk Yeol to convene a Cabinet meeting before the latter declared martial law. It upheld findings that some of Han’s actions after the declaration amounted to participation in the insurrection. Yang said the ruling had pushed the party’s patience to its limit. “We will not cite the substance of the ruling as a ground for impeachment,” he said. The task force will review allegations of serious procedural flaws in how the court heard the case, he added. The main opposition People Power Party (PPP) has called the impeachment push political retaliation. “Did the DPK decide to pursue impeachment first and only then look for grounds?” PPP chief spokesperson Rep. Choi Bo-yun said in a statement Sunday, accusing the DPK of deciding to pursue impeachment before establishing its grounds. She urged the ruling party to drop the effort, warning that impeaching Cho over a ruling backed by a majority of Supreme Court justices would undermine judicial independence. “It was a very emotional decision,” said Lee Jong-hoon, a political commentator and adviser at Daeryun Law Firm, referring to the DPK’s decision to pursue impeachment after the ruling in Han’s case. Lee said DPK leader Kim Min-seok had previously urged the party to hold a parliamentary inquiry first and give impeachment more thought. “I thought the Supreme Court got it right,” Lee said of the court’s judgment on Han’s actions before martial law was declared. Dispute over vacant seat The dispute over the vacant seat turns on whether the president can require the chief justice to recommend a different candidate. Under the Constitution, the president appoints Supreme Court justices on the chief justice’s recommendation and with the Assembly’s consent. The DPK argues that Cho’s refusal to put forward another candidate infringed on the president’s appointment power. In a statement opposing the DPK’s earlier push for a parliamentary inquiry into Cho, Kim Hyun, standing representative of People Making Good Laws, argued that the Constitution imposes no duty on the chief justice to consult the president in advance or recommend a replacement candidate. “Raising the prospect of an inquiry and impeachment over the exercise of a constitutional power amounts to political pressure on the chief justice to exercise his nominating authority in line with the president’s wishes,” Kim said. The rift between Lee and Cho dates back to the 2025 presidential campaign. On May 1, 2025, just over a month before the election, the Supreme Court’s full bench overturned an appeals court ruling that had acquitted Lee, then the DPK candidate, of violating the Public Official Election Act. It sent the case back to the Seoul High Court. The DPK accused the court of rushing the case to influence the vote. The court said it had reviewed the case swiftly and thoroughly in keeping with election law. The two clashed again in August, when Cho recommended Sohn Bong-ki, a senior judge at the Daegu District Court, for a Supreme Court seat. The presidential office declined to submit the nomination to the Assembly for confirmation and asked Cho to put forward another candidate. Cho rejected the request in September, saying the presidential office had failed to give a specific reason or identify a constitutional basis for it. The presidential office countered that his interpretation infringed on the president’s appointment power. Read More Why president, chief justice are clashing over Supreme Court seat

articles.summary: After leaving the Palace of Justice, the students said the proceedings had been legally unfounded and politically motivated
articles.body: Court proceedings against nine students accused of calling for a violent change to Serbia’s constitutional order were formally concluded on Friday at Belgrade’s Palace of Justice, after the prosecution dropped the charges due to insufficient evidence. After leaving the Palace of Justice, the students said the proceedings had been legally unfounded and politically motivated . “It is not enough that the proceedings have been discontinued. We should never have had to wait a year and a half for justice. Justice must not depend on the will of those in power, but on the law. We would like this to mark the beginning of a new chapter – one in which the rule of law is restored to institutions and the state is returned to the people,” one student, Dimitrije Stefanovic, said after the court session. Ivana Milenkovic, another defendant, called for accountability for all those who she said had participated in the arrests of her and her colleagues in an “unlawful and humiliating manner”. “From plainclothes police officers to prosecutors, no one can or should be above the law. As the saying goes, let justice take its course. After all, they know very well what they did,” Milenkovic said outside the Palace of Justice following the hearing. The nine students were arrested on June 29, 2025, a day after a major anti-government protest in Belgrade. They were accused of planning to radicalise the protests during meetings at the Faculty of Civil Engineering and the Faculty of Philology earlier that month. Ahead of the protest, secretly recorded conversations from these meetings were broadcast on pro-government television channels. According to the prosecution, the students had discussed plans to blockade several state institutions, among other locations. On September 11, 2026, the Higher Court in Belgrade ruled that evidence obtained through secret surveillance by Serbia’s Security Intelligence Agency, BIA, had been collected unlawfully and should be excluded from the case. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in October. On November 9, the Higher Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said it had dropped the charges. According to the prosecution, the excluded evidence constituted a significant part of its case, and the remaining material was insufficient to support a justified suspicion that the students had committed the alleged offences. The students’ lawyer Aleksandar Radojicic, told N1 TV on Friday that it was rare for prosecutors to drop charges and that he hoped this would mark “the final act of the drama that the outgoing regime created against the children”. Radojicic added that the judiciary had “shown integrity”, but there was still a “bitter taste” because they had not been able to hear the truth in the courtroom.

articles.title: Former Ally of Albania’s PM Rama Denounces Ruling Party’s Governance
articles.summary: Then Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali at a press conference in Tirana, February 2026
articles.body: Then Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali at a press conference in Tirana, February 2026. Photo: EPA/MALTON DIBRA. Former Foreign Minister Elisa Spiropali, once a close ally of Prime Minister Edi Rama, spoke out publicly against her own Socialist Party in a TV interview on Thursday evening after she was reportedly dismissed from all party structures at the Socialists’ general assembly on November 14. “I joined the Socialist Party, as a reformist force to change Albania; but what is the value of that today?” Spiropali, who was also speaker of the Albanian parliament between 2024 and 2025, said in the interview with Top Channel TV . The Socialist Party came to power in 2013 and Spiropali was a key figure until March this year, when she refused to follow Rama’s line on the scandal around Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Infrastructure Belinda Balluku, who was charged with interfering with public procurements and corruption. The Special Anti-Corruption Prosecution called on parliament to remove Balluku’s immunity to allow for her arrest. Reportedly, one day before the parliamentary vote on Balluku’s immunity, Rama ordered his MPs to vote against the prosecution’s request. However, Spiropali did not participate in the vote. In the interview with Top Channel’s ‘Top Story’ programme, Spiropali described the Balluku incident as “the worst example of governance by our political force”, and said the now-ousted minister was “the latest victim of a model that must change”. “This is what I believed when I chose not to go to parliament to vote on the immunity issue,” she said. Interviewer Grida Duma asked Spiropali how Balluku could represent the “worst example” and also be a victim. Spiropali responded: “At a time when power becomes so personalised that all filters and internal checks within a political force vanish, and it is now abundantly clear that political courage has disappeared, that there is no longer any willingness to raise issues for discussion within party forums, and that no one confronts significant matters concerning governance or the Socialist Party, then, inevitably, a pattern emerges defined by phone calls, text messages, arbitrary personal choices and grave errors.” Spiropali claimed that Balluku still maintains some power within the party because all its internal democratic mechanisms have failed. She declared: “We can no longer continue with people in political forums who are using the Socialist Party as a shield for their own personal predicaments. The Socialist Party is not a bunker where they can hide.” Asked if she had personally come under political pressure, she said: “From morning till night.” Asked by whom, she replied: “By Belinda Balluku and the institutions of this state.” Balluku has not responded publicly to these allegations. She has however denied wrongdoing in the corruption case. Rama has made no comment on Spiropali’s interview so far.

articles.title: House Democrats split over risking lame-duck shutdown to defund Iran war
articles.summary: We’re going to fight to get that Iran funding removed for offensive military capability,” said Rep
articles.body: House Democrats are wrestling with a lame-duck strategy on the Iran war, divided over whether to demand an end to war funding, which could risk triggering a government shutdown — or punting that fight to next year, when they’ll control Congress. On one side of the debate are liberals who, emboldened by this month’s midterm landslide, want to use the Democrats’ leverage in the government funding battle to deny the Pentagon any more money to conduct the war. “We’re going to fight to get that Iran funding removed for offensive military capability,” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). On the other side are top Democrats, including the lead negotiators on the spending package, who also oppose the war but aren’t ready to shutter the government over defunding it. “I frankly want to … end the funding to the Iran War. But shutting the government down doesn’t stop the war,” said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (Conn.), the senior Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. That internal clash has been playing out for several weeks on the other side of the Capitol, where Senate Democrats are also at odds over how aggressively to pursue the defund-the-war strategy in the lame duck session — a debate that’s grown only more salient after Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) launched a challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the top leadership spot next year. Van Hollen has positioned himself to the left of Schumer, and his demand to halt war funding immediately — even if it leads to a government shutdown — has energized the Democrats’ liberal base even as it has divided the party on Capitol Hill. The midterm results have fueled that clash, providing the Van Hollen camp with a powerful argument: Voters demanded this. The divisions on the House side have, so far, been less prominent. But as the government spending debate inches closer to the Dec. 11 shutdown deadline, liberals in the lower chamber are making clear that they’re on Van Hollen’s side, ready to oppose any spending package that continues to fund the Iran conflict. Asked if the issue is a red line, Khanna, a vice chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, didn’t hesitate. “Yes,” he said. “I do think we’ve got to get that money out.” DeLauro disagreed, arguing that Democrats will fight to end the war, but won’t die on that hill in the lame duck — not least because she doesn’t want a shutdown to delay the Democrats’ legislative agenda in January when they will take control of both chambers of Congress. “It’s not a red line,” she said. “I think we’re trying to get done what we can get done. Because we have a very important agenda to address — affordability and accountability — and we’re ready to do that. And I do not want to delay that.” DeLauro suggested Democrats are eying other strategies for ending the war that don’t risk a shutdown. She did not specify what those are, however, and many Democrats view Congress’s power of the purse as the most forceful tool they have at their disposal. “They want to end this war, and they want to see an end to the funding. The other issue is: How do you strategically move to get that done?” she said. “And that’s what we’re looking at — without shutting down the government.” Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), who’s in line to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee next year, has been a part of those talks. He suggested Democrats are searching for ways to restrict President Trump’s military operations against Iran in lieu of a complete defunding, which would likely be opposed by Republicans and could trigger a shutdown. “She’s working very hard to get this thing resolved, understanding that we just can’t give the president a blank check,” Meeks said of DeLauro. “You can’t [have a shutdown]. But having amendments and having conditions I think are important also, understanding that come the 120th Congress, we’re in full control, and right now we’re not.” “So we’ve got to figure it out.” That strategy would anger the Democrats’ activist base, who are clamoring for an immediate end to an unpopular war that was a major factor driving the midterm rout. But top Democrats say it’s also the most pragmatic route, empowering Democrats to hit the ground running — and not be bogged down in shutdown politics — when they do take power in January. “You’re going to have to get to the point where you defund it. I would like it to be in the lame duck. But, again, we have to see what are the options here, and what’s moving and what’s not moving,” said Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.). “Starting the new Congress with a government shutdown is not a good idea.” Iran funding is not the only sticking point that’s complicating the government funding negotiations and heightening the risk of a shutdown. Separately, the parties are also at odds over how long a stop-gap spending package, known as a continuing resolution, or CR, should extend into next year. Republicans, who are bracing to lose control of both chambers in the next Congress, want to extend funding at current levels for as long as possible while they still have their majorities in the lame duck. “I would be more in favor of the continuing resolution through the end of the fiscal year,” said Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a conservative who’s vying to lead the far-right House Freedom Caucus in the next Congress. “Longer term,” he continued, “because — just because we do a continuing resolution doesn’t mean we can’t come back and do appropriations.” Democrats, who will take their gavels in January, want a much shorter window, allowing them more power to dictate the terms of government spending for a longer stretch of 2027. “I want a CR that just goes to February — the shortest CR we can do so that we can get all the other business done,” DeLauro said.

articles.body: Vice President Vance dodged the question on Friday of whether he thought the Iran war was worth Republicans losing big in the midterm elections earlier this month. “The president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said at a press briefing alongside President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “What I've said is the goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we should be doing,” he said. “It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage, or God forbid, they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands, potentially of innocent people.” When pressed on whether he thinks it was worth it, Vance said: “My view is that my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States. Vance, in a lengthy post to the social platform X after the midterms, blamed the ongoing Iran war for Republicans' loss of the House and Senate to Democrats. “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on social media. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” he continued. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Trump said Friday that he had “no problem” with Vance’s social media post, adding that it was “very accurate,” but he said he would’ve added that he would have started the Iran war all over again despite the losses. “I thought the statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing, that I would have said that, ‘Would you do it again?’ And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

articles.title: Tillis blocks Trump cybersecurity nominee who refused to acknowledge Jan. 6 attack
articles.summary: Tillis said the question of whether the Capitol was attacked on Jan
articles.body: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) says he won’t allow President Trump’s nominee to serve as director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (CISA) to advance because he refused in a hearing to acknowledge the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the United States Capitol. Tillis said the question of whether the Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6 by a mob of Trump supporters seeking to stop the certification of former President Biden’s victory in the presidential election is a black-and-white issue. “It’s binary. The minute you pretend like it didn’t exist or you can’t even acknowledge it, I don’t have any time because it’s not a very thoughtful person,” Tillis told The Hill. Michael LoSapio, a former executive at Palantir, declined to call Jan. 6 an attack, even though many lawmakers in both parties who were on Capitol Hill that day say there’s no question the Capitol was attacked. When Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) asked the nominee at a Homeland Security Committee hearing whether there was “an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021,” LoSapio hesitated. “I, I don’t know,” he said. Blumenthal reacted with disbelief. “You don’t know?” he pressed the nominee. “Really?” “No, I don’t believe it was an attack, no,” LoSapio replied, adding that he “wasn’t involved in politics.” Blumenthal immediately rejected that excuse. “You weren’t involved in politics? Were you alive on this planet?” he demanded. “I was,” LoSapio responded. Blumenthal gave him a second chance to answer the question. “Let me ask you again, I’ll give you another chance,” the Connecticut senator said. “Jan. 6, 2021, was the Capitol attacked?” “No,” LoSapio said. “It was not attacked?” Blumenthal asked. “No, sir,” LoSapio responded. The role of CISA director has taken on new prominence because of recent technical outages that caused Microsoft Outlook to shut down last week and a nationwide ground stop of aircraft that the Federal Aviation Administration imposed last week, amid other high-profile glitches. Some cybersecurity experts have warned that cyberattacks cannot be ruled out as a potential cause even while federal officials say they have not yet uncovered any evidence of attacks.

editorialRejections.title: Hungary plans to withdraw its blockade of Ukraine’s EU accession talks

editorialRejections.body: After the long-standing blockade by Budapest, Hungary has agreed to withdraw its objections to the opening of the last two negotiating clusters with Ukraine, diplomatic sources confirmed. This opens the possibility for Kyiv and Chisinau to begin negotiations on all membership chapters in the European Union, Euronews reported. According to two diplomatic sources, Hungary plans to drop the veto at the meeting of the ambassadors of the EU member states. The intention was announced by Andras Biro-Nagy, state secretary for EU affairs, during the debate on enlargement in Brussels. Budapest had long blocked Ukraine’s candidacy, thereby also slowing the progress of Moldova, whose accession process was linked to the Ukrainian one. The change of position comes after Peter Magyar took power from Viktor Orban, who had been at the head of the Hungarian government for 16 years, Skopje1.mk reported. The first negotiating cluster was opened in June, the second in July, and the next two in October. Last month, Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement on the rights of the Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which was then adopted in the Ukrainian parliament. Although the Hungarian government announced readiness for the next step, the opening of the last two clusters was postponed for several weeks. Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held their first bilateral meeting in Brussels on 16 October, on the margins of the European Council summit, which represented an additional step toward improving relations between the two neighboring countries. Among the clusters that are to be opened are also sensitive areas such as the environment and agriculture. Agriculture in particular will be an especially big challenge for Ukraine. The European Commission, under pressure from countries such as Poland and France, proposed restrictions on the access of certain Ukrainian agricultural products to the European market and EU funds. Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretky stated that Kyiv cannot accept the permanent exclusion of Ukrainian farmers from the European market and emphasized that any restrictions must be temporary and proportional. The opening of the negotiating clusters is only the beginning of the accession process. The candidates then have to align their laws and practices with European rules, and the EU member states have more than a hundred opportunities in the further phases to impose a veto and block progress.

editorialRejections.body: Poland's government said Russian missiles landed in the country overnight as Vladimir Putin's forces hammered Ukraine with what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called "one of the largest attacks" since the war began. The strikes on Ukraine killed at least eight people, according to Zelenskyy.The prime minister of Poland, a NATO member, decried the Russian weapons landing in his country as "an intentional provocation" of the U.S.-led military alliance."We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia. Therefore — ⁠and this is not just my own assessment, but ‌also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an ‌accident," Prime Minister ⁠Donald Tusk said. "It ‌appears that we ⁠are dealing with an intentional ⁠provocation."NATO and Allied planes responded to the incident, including Polish F-16s, Swedish JAS 39 Gripens, a Dutch A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) aerial refueling aircraft and others. NATO and Allied ground-based air defenses were also alerted."Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote, adding that Putin's attempt to "redraw the world" with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts during their summit Thursday in China had been a "failure.""Hard to regard it as a coincidence"Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine overnight and early Friday, including cluster munitions, Zelenskyy said in a fiery social media post. Some of the Russian weapons hit the Austrian embassy and landed near the Netherlands embassy in Kyiv, prompting France to call for a meeting of the United Nations Security Council."Russia will have to answer for this," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote in a social media post.Poland's defense minister said three Russian weapons, believed to have been two missiles and a drone, entered southeast Poland's airspace on Friday. Poland scrambled fighter jets and Patriot anti-missile systems in the country's southeast were activated, but no injuries were reported.Drones have repeatedly entered the airspace of Poland and other NATO countries, mostly near Ukraine but not all, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022.The Article 5 collective defense clause in NATO's founding charter states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all 32.NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said in a Friday social media post that he had spoken with Tusk "about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight" and stressed that the alliance stands "in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.""This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte said. "I condemn Russia's attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine."NATO's Supreme Allied Commander for Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, was in "close contact with Poland's chief of defense and minister of defense as Poland's investigation into the overnight airspace violations continues," his spokesperson Martin O'Donnell told CBS News on Friday.Thousands of troops from 11 European countries that support Kyiv, members of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, are currently in Poland taking part in a major military exercise framed as training for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine. According to Polish defense officials, two missiles thought to be Russian Kh-101s and one jet-powered drone landed between 30 and 60 miles inside Polish territory from the border with Ukraine. "It is hard to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincide with the Coalition of the Willing's exercises," Deputy Polish Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote in a social media post.The escalation comes a day after President Trump sat with Xi and Putin — whom he greeted warmly and called his friend — in Shenzhen, China, for a rare face-to-face meeting that seemed to achieve little.The presidents discussed the Ukraine war, which Mr. Trump has long pushed to end through negotiations, but soon after the 90-minute meeting, Putin ruled out direct talks with Kyiv, citing a strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces that severely damaged a highly symbolic bridge linking Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula. "We will respond to these strikes," Putin warned Thursday. "I want everyone to know this. I believe that our retaliatory actions … will be far more painful than what the Kiev regime did to the bridge."At least 8 killed, dozens wounded in UkraineUkrainian forces managed to intercept 79 of the 110 missiles Russia launched overnight, Zelenskyy said, but none of the 27 ballistic missiles, which he attributed to Kyiv's lack of interceptors. He has been pleading with the Trump administration to help Ukraine replenish its missile interceptor stocks for months, saying the shortage is being paid for in civilian lives.Russia's attack targeted Kyiv and nine other regions, leaving more than two dozen people wounded in addition to the eight confirmed to have been killed, according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi."Missiles hit critical infrastructure in the capital, including bridges," he said. "A water supply facility, office and commercial buildings were damaged."A hospital in Kharkiv was damaged, as well as businesses in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Chernihiv regions, and residential buildings in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Sumy, Chernihiv and Lviv, which is in the far west, close to Poland, Koretskyi said, adding that energy infrastructure was also hit.Some nuclear plants were forced to reduce power generation after the attacks, according to an energy ministry official."The tactics of the strike this time were particularly vile," Zelenskyy said in his post on social media, noting that there had been "several groups of missiles with pauses of 20-30 minutes to complicate extinguishing the fires, clearing the rubble and recovery.""A clear response from the world to all this is also needed," he said. "It is important that there are not only statements from partners about supporting Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also the implementation of specific agreements on air defense … We very much hope that the Pentagon will release the supply that we expect."
